metrics = {'T_median': 100.0, 'T_median_ok': True, 'T_median_ratio': 1.0, 'contaminated_files': {}, ...}

reference_data_stats = {'chance_majority': {'choice': 0.5080657459406058, 'prior_probability_left': 0.4414379769663778, 'wheel_speed': 0.3334...33333333333}, 'data_summary': {'T_max': 100, 'T_mean': 100.0, 'T_median': 100.0, 'T_min': 100, ...}, 'errors': [], ...}

    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):
            metrics['input_range_ok'] = bool(
                mean_input_range_error <= STATLIMITS['input_range_error'])
    
        # match outputs based on range, fraction, and semantic similarity of names
        output_matches, output_match_costs = match_outputs(
            submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
        )
        metrics['output_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in output_matches
        ]
    
        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))
        metrics['output_match_mean_cost'] = mean_output_match_cost
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats['output_range']
        ref_output_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_output_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None
        try:
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
    
        # evaluate accuracy on test set
        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)
        balanced_accuracy = accuracy_all_sessions(test_predictions_only, test_output_only, balanced=True)
    
        sub_accuracy = {
            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])
            for i in range(len(balanced_accuracy))
        }
        # Persist the raw per-output accuracy as soon as it's computed. Everything
        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be
        # required to preserve this field.
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison, skipping accuracy ratio and threshold checks")
            return
    
        # The matching + ratio + threshold checks below are wrapped so that a
        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.
        # Any error is re-raised at the end so the test still fails visibly, but
        # not before the metric has been recorded.
        deferred_error = None
        try:
            # find a match between output dimensions (same as test_data_stats)
            output_matches, _ = match_outputs(
                submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
            )
            # The mean of those costs is deliberately NOT recorded here. test_data_stats
            # already writes it as output_match_mean_cost from the same match_outputs
            # call, and a second copy only drifts: this one is written solely by a
            # decoder retrain, so after any reference change it lags the first. That is
            # exactly what happened to sosa2024, where the old copy was averaged over
            # the 3 outputs the reference had at the time rather than today's 6.
    
            # Best-effort ratio: skip any match whose reference or submitted name
            # isn't resolvable (e.g. matcher returned inf cost / None).
            ratio = {}
            for ref_name, sub_name, cost in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy or not ref_accuracy[ref_name]:
                    continue
                ratio[ref_name] = sub_accuracy[sub_name] / ref_accuracy[ref_name]
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio
    
            # Recorded so a failure can be read without recomputing anything: the bar each
            # output had to clear.
            thresholds = {}
    
            # Two passes, deliberately. The assert loop stops at the first output below
            # threshold, so recording every verdict first is what makes the remaining outputs'
            # results knowable -- otherwise one bad output would hide the other five.
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                threshold = accuracy_threshold(ref_name, reference_data_stats)
                thresholds[ref_name] = threshold
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                    sub_accuracy[sub_name] >= threshold)
            # Written before the asserts, so a failing output's bar is on record too.
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_threshold'] = thresholds
    
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                sub_acc = sub_accuracy[sub_name]
                threshold = thresholds[ref_name]
                mean = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_mean'][ref_name]
                std = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_std'][ref_name]
                assert metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'], (
                    f'Accuracy for output {sub_name} ({sub_acc:.3f}) is below reference mean '
                    f'{mean:.3f} - {ACCURACY_NSTD:g}*std {std:.3f} = {threshold:.3f}')
        except BaseException as e:  # AssertionError or anything raised by the matcher
            deferred_error = e
    
        if deferred_error is not None:

For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\n/app/methods.txt:13:For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\n/app/methods.txt:17:We focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.\n/app/methods.txt:21:We trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\n/app/methods.txt:35:The automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.\n/app/methods.txt:44:Sessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).\n/app/methods.txt:51:For the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.\n/app/methods.txt:66:We performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). For each kept trial, the spikes falling in `[onset-0.5, onset+1.5)` are sliced with `searchsorted`, assigned a bin index by `floor((t-edges[0])/0.02)`, and counted with a single flat `bincount` into an (n_clusters, 100) matrix. The values stored are raw **spike counts per 20 ms bin** (not rates), clipped at 255 and cast to `uint8`. No smoothing, no z-scoring, no firing-rate conversion.\n\nii.\n```python\nt=np.concatenate(times); c=np.concatenate(clus)\norder=np.argsort(t,kind='mergesort')\nreturn t[order],c[order],regions\n```\n```python\nonset=tr['stimOn_times'][j]; edges=onset+OFF0+np.arange(NBIN+1)*BIN\nlo=np.searchsorted(st,edges[0],'left'); hi=np.searchsorted(st,edges[-1],'left')\ntt=st[lo:hi]; cc=sc[lo:hi]\ntb=np.floor((tt-edges[0])/BIN).astype(np.int64)\nflat=cc*NBIN+tb\ncounts=np.bincount(flat,minlength=ncl*NBIN).reshape(ncl,NBIN)\ncounts=np.minimum(counts,255).astype(np.uint8)\n```\n\niii. \"The reference configuration is confirmed as 100 time bins at 20 ms over [-0.5, 1.5] s around `stimOn_times`\", and probes are merged because the reference does so (its `merge_probes` docstring: probes in one session are not statistically independent). `uint8` counts were chosen explicitly for size: \"Large sessions are handled with compact uint8 spike-count matrices\". The validator warned 189,315 times that neural dtype is `uint8` rather than float32, but converts at training time.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. **No quality-control filter is applied.** Every sorted cluster of every released probe is kept, including MUA/noise-labelled clusters and clusters whose histology places them outside the brain (`void`/`root`); only clusters with an out-of-range id are dropped (`0 <= id < n_clusters`, which never removes anything in practice). The result is 600,174 neurons over 445 sessions (mean 1,349, max 3,140 per session), versus 72,422 (mean 164) for the expert reference, and a 26.7 GB pickle.\n\nii.\n```python\n# Cluster IDs index the merged table. Keep all clusters as in prepare_data(qc=None).\nn=len(merged); valid=(sc>=0)&(sc<n)\n```\n```python\n'neural_measure':'spike counts per 20 ms bin; all release clusters (reference qc=None)',\n```\n\niii. This was an explicit, investigated decision. The AI first planned strict QC (\"load/merge release probes with `SpikeSortingLoader` QC label >= 1\"), then checked the numbers on the example probe (\"898 total clusters but only 76 with the strict IBL QC label of 1\") and said \"the task explicitly requires matching reference curation; we must verify whether the methods code uses that strict label\". It then grepped the actual call site and concluded: \"The reference `prepare_data` deliberately loads all clusters (`qc=None`), not only label-1 units; therefore the converter should retain all clusters from the BWM release probes.\" This is consistent with `/app/methods.txt`, which says the method paper bins \"spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5, from each session\".\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. All IBL streams are already on one synchronised session clock, so alignment is just building the bin edges from each trial's `stimOn_times`: `edges = stimOn_times + (-0.5) + k*0.02`, k = 0..100. Spikes are sliced by absolute time between the first and last edge and binned relative to `edges[0]`, which puts bin 0 at 500 ms before stimulus onset and bin 99 ending 1.5 s after it. No resampling or cross-stream clock correction is done.\n\nii.\n```python\nonset=tr['stimOn_times'][j]; edges=onset+OFF0+np.arange(NBIN+1)*BIN\nlo=np.searchsorted(st,edges[0],'left'); hi=np.searchsorted(st,edges[-1],'left')\ntb=np.floor((tt-edges[0])/BIN).astype(np.int64)\n```\n```python\n'temporal_alignment_event':'visual stimulus onset (stimOn_times)','off_start':-0.5,'off_end':1.5,\n```\n\niii. \"The reference configuration is confirmed as 100 time bins at 20 ms over [-0.5, 1.5] s around `stimOn_times`\" — taken from the reference decoding config and from `/app/methods.txt` (\"For choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset\"), which is also what the task instructions ask for.\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 20 ms bins, 100 bins per trial, identical for every trial and session; `metadata['time_bin_size'] = 20.0` ms. Spikes are binned once directly at 20 ms, so there is no rebinning or interpolation of the neural data. (The method paper uses 50 ms for choice/prior and 20 ms for the dynamic behaviours; the AI used 20 ms throughout, as the target format requires a single bin size.)\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN=.02; OFF0=-.5; OFF1=1.5; NBIN=100\nCENTERS=np.arange(NBIN,dtype=np.float64)*BIN + OFF0 + BIN/2\n...\n'time_bin_size':20.0,\n```\n\niii. Same as 2-d: the 20 ms / 100-bin configuration was read off the reference code and methods text and confirmed against the validator.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time since stimulus onset* derived from?\n\ni. It is not derived from raw data at all — it is the fixed bin-centre grid defined by the analysis window (`-0.5 + 0.02k + 0.01`, giving -0.49 … 1.49 s). It is implicitly tied to `stimOn_times`, the event the window is anchored on, and is the same vector for every trial of every session.\n\nii.\n```python\nCENTERS=np.arange(NBIN,dtype=np.float64)*BIN + OFF0 + BIN/2\n...\ninp=np.vstack((CENTERS.astype(np.float32),np.full(NBIN,blockno[j],np.float32)))\n```\n\niii. No separate justification; it falls out of the alignment window chosen in 2-d.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time since stimulus onset*?\n\ni. None. The constant `CENTERS` vector is cast to float32 and stacked as row 0 of the (2, 100) input array for every trial.\n\nii.\n```python\ninp=np.vstack((CENTERS.astype(np.float32),np.full(NBIN,blockno[j],np.float32)))\n```\n```python\n'input_names':['time since stimulus onset','trial number in block'],\n```\n\niii. N/A.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time since stimulus onset* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is the centre of exactly the same bins the spikes are counted into: the neural bin edges are `onset + OFF0 + k*BIN` and `CENTERS[k] = OFF0 + k*BIN + BIN/2`, so input column k and neural column k describe the same 20 ms interval. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Trial number in block* derived from?\n\ni. From `probabilityLeft` in the trials table only. Because the block prior is constant within a block, a change in its value marks a block boundary; the trials table carries no explicit block id.\n\nii.\n```python\nprior_all=tr['probabilityLeft']; blockno=block_trial_numbers(prior_all)\n```\n\niii. No explicit statement in the trajectory; the AI noted early that the trials table contains \"the expected three prior levels\" and used them to recover blocks.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Trial number in block*?\n\ni. A running counter over **all** trials of the session (computed before the quality mask is applied, so dropped trials still advance the animal's true position in the block), reset to 0 whenever `probabilityLeft` differs from the previous trial, and 0 for the first trial. The scalar is broadcast across all 100 bins as row 1 of the input array. Observed range 0–98, matching the reference.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef block_trial_numbers(prior):\n    out=np.zeros(len(prior),np.float32); k=0\n    for i in range(1,len(prior)):\n        k = 0 if prior[i] != prior[i-1] else k+1\n        out[i]=k\n    return out\n...\ninp=np.vstack((CENTERS.astype(np.float32),np.full(NBIN,blockno[j],np.float32)))\n```\n\niii. Not discussed explicitly; the AI listed it among the \"categorical encodings required by the task\" and confirmed the resulting value range with the validator.\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Choice* derived from?\n\ni. The `choice` column of the trials table, which is +1 / -1 / 0. Trials with `choice == 0` (no response) are already removed by the mask. The AI maps `-1 → 0` and `+1 → 1`, and labels the classes `['left','right']`, i.e. it treats `choice == -1` as \"left\". In the IBL convention (`ibllib/brainbox/behavior/training.py`: `rightward = trials.choice == -1`, and `# choice == -1 means contrast on right hand side`) `choice == +1` is a leftward choice and `-1` is rightward, so this mapping is inverted relative to the instructions' `left = 0, right = 1`. The resulting class fractions (0: 0.4921, 1: 0.5079) are the mirror image of the reference's (0: 0.5075, 1: 0.4925).\n\nii.\n```python\nchoice=np.uint8(0 if tr['choice'][j] == -1 else 1)\n...\nout=np.empty((4,NBIN),np.float32); out[0]=choice; ...\n'output_values':[['left','right'], ...]\n```\n\niii. No justification is given anywhere — neither in the code (the line has no comment) nor in the trajectory, which only mentions \"encode choice and prior\" and excluding `choice == 0`. The sign convention was never checked against the IBL documentation or against `contrastLeft`/`feedbackType`.\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Choice*?\n\ni. Nothing beyond the recode described above: the per-trial scalar is broadcast across all 100 bins (row 0 of the (4, 100) output array) and finally cast to `uint8`, so choice is stored as a constant time series rather than a per-trial scalar.\n\nii.\n```python\nout=np.empty((4,NBIN),np.float32); out[0]=choice; out[1]=prior; out[2]=ws; out[3]=me\n...\n'output':[[o.astype(np.uint8) for o in s['output']] for s in sessions],\n```\n\niii. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Prior probability of left* derived from?\n\ni. Trials with a non-finite `probabilityLeft` are already excluded; a value outside the three expected ones would raise a `KeyError` and drop the whole session.\n\nii.\n```python\npv=float(prior_all[j]); prior=np.uint8({.2:0,.5:1,.8:2}[round(pv,1)])\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Prior probability of left*?\n\ni. None beyond the recode; the value is broadcast across the 100 bins as row 1 of the output array. Unbiased (0.5) blocks are retained, giving fractions 0.417 / 0.141 / 0.442, essentially identical to the reference (0.418 / 0.141 / 0.442).\n\nii.\n```python\nout[1]=prior\n```\n\niii. N/A.\n\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Wheel speed* derived from?\n\ni. The raw ALF wheel object, `wheel.timestamps` and `wheel.position` (radians), loaded directly with `one.load_object` rather than through `SessionLoader`.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef load_wheel(one,eid):\n    w=one.load_object(eid,'wheel',collection='alf')\n    t=np.asarray(w['timestamps'],float); p=np.asarray(w['position'],float)\n```\n\niii. \"Wheel velocity must be derived from position/timestamps\" — the AI chose not to use `SessionLoader` for any behavioural stream after `load_motion_energy` failed by trying to write into the read-only cache.\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Wheel speed*?\n\ni. Non-finite samples are dropped, non-monotonic/duplicate timestamps are dropped, and the speed is the absolute value of a **central difference of the raw encoder position against its irregular timestamps** (`np.abs(np.gradient(p, t))`). The trace is then sampled at the 100 bin centres of each trial with `np.interp`. This is *not* what the reference does: the reference's `load_target_behavior('wheel-speed')` takes `np.abs(SessionLoader.wheel['velocity'])`, and `SessionLoader.load_wheel` first interpolates position onto a uniform 1000 Hz grid and then differentiates it with a 20 Hz low-pass Butterworth filter. So the AI's speed is an unsmoothed, non-uniformly-sampled estimate of the same physical quantity; the code comment claims it matches \"SessionLoader's velocity meaning\", which is true of the units (rad/s) but not of the filtering.\n\nii.\n```python\nok=np.isfinite(t)&np.isfinite(p); t,p=t[ok],p[ok]\nu=np.r_[True,np.diff(t)>0]; t,p=t[u],p[u]\n# Central-difference angular velocity, matching SessionLoader's velocity meaning.\nspeed=np.abs(np.gradient(p,t))\n```\n```python\nx=onset+CENTERS\nws=np.interp(x,wt,wv).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. The stated reason for bypassing `SessionLoader` is in the module docstring: \"Existing ALF camera arrays are read directly because current SessionLoader tries to write derived features into the intentionally read-only source cache.\" That argument concerns the camera; the AI extended it to the wheel without separately testing whether `SessionLoader.load_wheel` (which computes in memory) would have worked, and without noting the loss of the 20 Hz filter.\n\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Wheel speed* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Three classes split at the **global** 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles computed over the concatenation of every trial of every session (18.9 M samples), not per session. The thresholds (0.0626 and ~0.4 rad/s) are stored in `metadata['behavior_bin_edges']`. Globally the three classes are exactly equal in size (0.3333 each), matching the reference's marginal fractions, but within an individual session the classes are not balanced.\n\nii.\n```python\nqw=np.quantile(np.concatenate([s['wheel'] for s in sessions]),[1/3,2/3])\n...\no[2]=np.digitize(o[2],qw).astype(np.float32)\n...\n'behavior_bin_edges':{'wheel_speed':qw.tolist(),'whisker_motion_energy':qm.tolist()},\n```\n\niii. \"Global finite tertiles give reproducible, balanced three-class behavior outputs\" (code comment); earlier the AI described this as \"quantile-discretize the two continuous behaviors into three global/session-consistent bins\", i.e. it explicitly wanted one common threshold so that the class label means the same physical speed in every session.\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Wheel speed* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Linear interpolation of the wheel-speed trace at `stimOn_times + CENTERS`, i.e. the centres of exactly the 100 bins the spikes are counted into, on the same session clock. Bin k of the output therefore corresponds to bin k of the neural matrix. Values outside the available wheel samples are not dropped — `np.interp` clamps to the first/last sample.\n\nii.\n```python\nx=onset+CENTERS\nws=np.interp(x,wt,wv).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. Follows directly from the shared bin grid; the AI stated its plan as \"interpolate wheel speed and left/right whisker motion energy onto bin centers\".\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Whisker motion energy* derived from?\n\ni. The released side-camera ROI motion energy, `<cam>Camera.ROIMotionEnergy.npy`, with frame times `_ibl_<cam>Camera.times.npy`. The left camera is used when it loads and has >2 finite samples, otherwise the right camera; the camera actually used is recorded per session in `metadata['session_info']`. 14 sessions had neither and were dropped.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef load_camera(one,eid):\n    # Reference uses left whisker ME and falls back to right if unavailable.\n    for cam in ('left','right'):\n        try:\n            t=np.asarray(one.load_dataset(eid,f'_ibl_{cam}Camera.times.npy',collection='alf'),float)\n            v=np.asarray(one.load_dataset(eid,f'{cam}Camera.ROIMotionEnergy.npy',collection='alf'),float).squeeze()\n            n=min(len(t),len(v)); t,v=t[:n],v[:n]\n            ok=np.isfinite(t)&np.isfinite(v)\n            if ok.sum()>2: return t[ok],v[ok],cam\n        except Exception: pass\n    raise RuntimeError('no whisker motion-energy stream')\n```\n\niii. The AI grepped the reference `bin_behaviors` and concluded: \"Whisker motion energy uses the left camera when available and falls back to right, rather than averaging cameras\" — an explicit correction of its own earlier plan to average the two cameras.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Whisker motion energy*?\n\ni. The released trace is used as-is: length-mismatch between times and values is truncated to the shorter, non-finite samples are dropped, and the trace is linearly interpolated onto the 100 bin centres of each trial. No filtering, normalisation or per-session standardisation before discretisation.\n\nii.\n```python\nme=np.interp(x,mt,mv).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. \"Direct stream inspection confirms camera motion energy can be loaded without SessionLoader and aligned by camera timestamps.\" The reference also uses the released `whiskerMotionEnergy` column unmodified.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Whisker motion energy* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Same rule as the wheel: three classes split at the global 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles pooled over all sessions, applied after the whole dataset has been converted. Note that this pools left-camera (60 Hz) and right-camera (150 Hz) motion energy, whose absolute values depend on the camera, the ROI size and the video resolution, into one set of thresholds.\n\nii.\n```python\nqm=np.quantile(np.concatenate([s['whisk'] for s in sessions]),[1/3,2/3])\n...\no[3]=np.digitize(o[3],qm).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. Same justification as 7-c: \"Global finite tertiles give reproducible, balanced three-class behavior outputs.\"\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Whisker motion energy* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Linear interpolation of the camera trace at `stimOn_times + CENTERS`, the same bin centres as the neural data and on the same session clock, so it shares the neural time axis bin for bin. As with the wheel, no check is made that the camera actually covers the trial window; outside its range `np.interp` clamps.\n\nii.\n```python\nx=onset+CENTERS\nme=np.interp(x,mt,mv).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. As 8-b: the camera timestamps are already on the session clock, so evaluating at the bin centres is all that is needed.\n\n## 9. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Several mechanisms, all \"drop and record\":\n- Trials with a non-finite value in any of the eight required trial fields are dropped (superset of the reference's `nan_exclude`).\n- Non-finite wheel or camera samples are dropped before interpolation; wheel samples with non-increasing timestamps are dropped; camera times/values of unequal length are truncated to the shorter.\n- A missing whisker stream falls back left → right, and if neither loads the whole session raises and is skipped.\n- Sessions with fewer than two valid trials, or with no release probes, raise and are skipped.\n- Every per-session exception is caught, emitted as a warning and appended to `failures`, which is written into `metadata['failed_sessions']` (14 sessions, all for a missing whisker stream).\n\nWhat is *not* handled: there is no check that the wheel/camera streams span the trial window, so a trial at the edge of a recording gets a silently flat, edge-clamped behavioural trace instead of being dropped (the reference code does apply such a check — \"target data starts too late\" / \"ends too early\" — and the expert reference implements it as `covered()`). Also `counts=np.minimum(counts,255)` silently clips, and a spike landing exactly on the last bin edge could in principle produce `tb == 100` and mis-attribute a count (or raise on reshape) rather than being clipped into the last bin.\n\nii.\n```python\nn=len(d['choice']); good=np.ones(n,bool)\nfor k in keys: good &= np.isfinite(d[k])\n```\n```python\nn=min(len(t),len(v)); t,v=t[:n],v[:n]\nok=np.isfinite(t)&np.isfinite(v)\nif ok.sum()>2: return t[ok],v[ok],cam\n```\n```python\nexcept Exception as ex:\n    warnings.warn(f'{eid}: {ex}'); failures.append((eid,repr(ex)))\n...\n'failed_sessions':failures\n```\n\niii. \"Fourteen sessions were excluded because required streams (notably whisker motion energy) were unavailable; this is appropriate because every requested output must be present and aligned.\" The AI also deliberately reviewed the failure list before assembly to check the exclusions were legitimate missing-data cases rather than loader bugs.\n\n## 10-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. (1) Reading the spike sorting: `sl.load_spike_sorting()` is called per probe with the default `SPIKES_ATTRIBUTES = ['clusters','times','amps','depths']`, so twice as many large arrays are read off the NFS cache as the conversion needs, and `merge_clusters` occasionally recomputes cluster metrics (the AI observed \"metric-computation progress bars\"). (2) The per-trial spike-binning loop, whose `bincount` is over `n_clusters * 100` entries — with all clusters kept this is up to 314,000 bins per trial for ~500 trials. (3) Serialisation: 445 session pickles are written and then read back, and a 26.7 GB final pickle is written — the dominant I/O cost, and a direct consequence of keeping all 600 k clusters. The AI measured ~8–9 sessions/min single-threaded (≈55 min total) and sharded the run across 8 background workers to cut it to a few minutes.\n\nii.\n```python\nsl=SpikeSortingLoader(one=one,pid=row.pid,eid=row.eid,pname=row.probe_name)\ns,c,ch=sl.load_spike_sorting()\nmerged=sl.merge_clusters(s,c,ch).to_df()\n```\n```python\ncounts=np.bincount(flat,minlength=ncl*NBIN).reshape(ncl,NBIN)\n```\n```python\ntmp=Path(args.output+'.tmp'); pickle.dump(data,open(tmp,'wb'),protocol=5); os.replace(tmp,args.output)\n```\n\niii. \"The sequential run has reached session 59. At the current rate, completing 459 sessions would take roughly another 45–55 minutes. Since sessions are independent and the host has ample CPU/RAM, conversion can be safely parallelized while retaining per-session atomic checkpoints.\" The AI then added `--shard`/`--cache-only` and ran 8 disjoint workers; it also chose `uint8` neural arrays specifically to keep the pickle manageable.\n\n## 10-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. Three.\n- The main per-trial loop in `convert_session`: the spike binning could be done for all trials at once with a single `bincount` whose flat index also encodes the trial (`trial*ncl*NBIN + cluster*NBIN + bin`), and the two `np.interp` calls could be replaced by one `np.interp` over the concatenated query vector `(stim_on[:,None] + CENTERS).ravel()` since both traces are monotone in time.\n- `block_trial_numbers` is a Python loop over every trial; it is a group-wise cumulative count and can be written vectorised (`(prior != shift(prior)).cumsum()` + `groupby(...).cumcount()`, as the expert reference does).\n- The final relabelling loop `for s in sessions: for o in s['output']` calls `np.digitize` once per trial (189,315 times) on a 2×100 slice; it could digitize a whole session's stacked behaviour at once.\n\nii.\n```python\nfor j in idx:\n    ...\n    counts=np.bincount(flat,minlength=ncl*NBIN).reshape(ncl,NBIN)\n    ws=np.interp(x,wt,wv).astype(np.float32)\n    me=np.interp(x,mt,mv).astype(np.float32)\n```\n```python\ndef block_trial_numbers(prior):\n    out=np.zeros(len(prior),np.float32); k=0\n    for i in range(1,len(prior)):\n        k = 0 if prior[i] != prior[i-1] else k+1\n```\n```python\nfor s in sessions:\n    for o in s['output']:\n        o[2]=np.digitize(o[2],qw).astype(np.float32); o[3]=np.digitize(o[3],qm).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. Not discussed. The AI addressed throughput by process-level parallelism (8 shards) rather than vectorisation.\n\n## 10-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni.\n- Every session is pickled to `/app/session_cache/<eid>.pkl` and then, in the assembly pass, read back and re-pickled into the 26.7 GB output — the full dataset is serialised and deserialised twice, and both copies stay on disk.\n- The behavioural traces are stored twice per session: once inside `output` rows 2/3 and once again in the flat `s['wheel']` / `s['whisk']` arrays kept only to compute the global quantiles.\n- The output arrays are cast to `uint8` twice, once in-place into the float32 buffer and once when the dict is built.\n- `rel[rel.eid==eid]` rescans the 699-row release table once per session (cheap, but a `groupby` would do it once).\n- The per-trial `np.searchsorted` on the full spike array is repeated per trial rather than computed once for all trial boundaries.\n\nii.\n```python\ntmp=f.with_suffix('.tmp'); pickle.dump(s,open(tmp,'wb'),protocol=5); os.replace(tmp,f)\n...\nfor eid in eids:\n    f=CACHE/f'{eid}.pkl'\n    if f.exists(): sessions.append(pickle.load(open(f,'rb')))\n```\n```python\nreturn {... Globally the three classes are exactly equal in size (0.3333 each), matching the reference's marginal fractions, but within an individual session the classes are not balanced.\n\nii.\n```python\nqw=np.quantile(np.concatenate([s['wheel'] for s in sessions]),[1/3,2/3])\n...\no[2]=np.digitize(o[2],qw).astype(np.float32)\n...\n'behavior_bin_edges':{'wheel_speed':qw.tolist(),'whisker_motion_energy':qm.tolist()},\n```\n\niii. \"Global finite tertiles give reproducible, balanced three-class behavior outputs\" (code comment); earlier the AI described this as \"quantile-discretize the two continuous behaviors into three global/session-consistent bins\", i.e. it explicitly wanted one common threshold so that the class label means the same physical speed in every session.\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Wheel speed* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Linear interpolation of the wheel-speed trace at `stimOn_times + CENTERS`, i.e. the centres of exactly the 100 bins the spikes are counted into, on the same session clock. Values outside the available wheel samples are not dropped — `np.interp` clamps to the first/last sample.\n\nii.\n```python\nx=onset+CENTERS\nws=np.interp(x,wt,wv).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. The released trace is used as-is: length-mismatch between times and values is truncated to the shorter, non-finite samples are dropped, and the trace is linearly interpolated onto the 100 bin centres of each trial. The count is taken before the reaction time and no response filters are applied, so a trial that is later dropped still advances it and the number is the animal's real position in the block.\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *choice* derived from?\n\ni. One column of the trials table, `choice`, which is +1, -1 or 0. It is recoded to 0 for left and 1 for right, and the 0 entries, meaning the animal did not respond, are dropped with the trial.\n\nii. The mapping, and where it is applied:\n```python\nCHOICE = {1.0: 0, -1.0: 1}       # +1 is a leftward choice, -1 rightward; 0 is a no response, dropped\n```\n\n```python\n'choice': trials.choice.map(CHOICE),\n```\n\niii. The IBL uses +1 for left choice and -1 for rightward choice. No response trials are dropped.\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *choice*?\n\ni. None beyond the recoding of +1 and -1 to 0 and 1 described above.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *prior_probability_left* derived from?\n\ni. One column of the trials table, `probabilityLeft`, which takes the three values 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 and is recoded to 0, 1 and 2.\n\nii. The mapping, and where it is applied:\n```python\nPRIOR = {0.2: 0, 0.5: 1, 0.8: 2}\n```\n\n```python\n'prior': trials.probabilityLeft.map(PRIOR),\n```\n\niii. The three values are the block prior the task holds constant within a block, and the instructions give this mapping.\n\n## 6-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *prior_probability_left*?\n\ni. None beyond the recoding of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 to 0, 1 and 2 described above.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *wheel_speed* derived from?\n\ni. The wheel position and its timestamps, `_ibl_wheel.position` and `_ibl_wheel.timestamps`. `SessionLoader` turns them into a velocity, and the speed is the absolute value of that velocity.\n\nii. The wheel, and the speed taken from it:\n```python\nloader.load_wheel()\n```\n\n```python\n\"\"\"Convert the IBL brain-wide map into the decoder format.\n\nUsage: python -u convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full | --sample] [--datadir DIR]\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport datetime\nimport os\nimport pickle\nimport time\nimport warnings\nfrom concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, as_completed\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\nfrom tqdm import tqdm\n\n_zhang2025_seed = 'x5cidj2hy87s'\nnp.random.seed(sum(ord(c) for c in _zhang2025_seed) % 2**31)\n\n# the loader always pulls these four spike arrays\nimport brainbox.io.one as bio\nbio.SPIKES_ATTRIBUTES = ['clusters', 'times']\n\nfrom one.api import ONE, One\nfrom one.alf.exceptions import ALFWarning\nfrom brainbox.io.one import SessionLoader, SpikeSortingLoader\nfrom iblatlas.regions import BrainRegions\n\n# the trials table and the spike sorting are each listed at two revisions, and ONE warns\n# once per load that it is taking the later one, which is the one we want\nwarnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=ALFWarning)\n\n# --- constants ---\n\nHERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))\n# Directory holding the one_cache/ folder. Harbor mounts the dataset at /app/data while\n# this script runs from /solution, so solve.sh overrides this with --datadir.\nDATA_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, 'data')\nRELEASE = 'Brainwidemap'\nONE_CACHE_DIRNAME = 'one_cache'\nBASE_URL = 'https://openalyx.internationalbrainlab.org'\nPASSWORD = 'international'\n# ONE expires a cached REST response five minutes after it is written. The cache shipped\n# with the dataset is pre-dated so it survives; this keeps what this run caches alive too.\nREST_EXPIRY = datetime.timedelta(days=365 * 50)\n\nT_START, T_STOP = -0.5, 1.5      # decoding window around stimulus onset, following the reference code\nBIN = 0.02\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))            # 100\nEDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)\nTIME = EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                              # bin centres, the first decoder input\n\n# reaction time bounds of the paper, which truncates the distribution at 80 ms and 2 s;\nMIN_RT, MAX_RT = 0.08, 2.0\n\nQC_LABEL = 1.0                   # the \"stringent quality control\" of the paper, 75,708 units of 621,733\nSPLIT = [100 / 3, 2 * 100 / 3]       # equal sized classes, from percentiles of each session's own trace\n\nCHOICE = {1.0: 0, -1.0: 1}       # +1 is a leftward choice, -1 rightward; 0 is a no response, dropped\nPRIOR = {0.2: 0, 0.5: 1, 0.8: 2}\nMOVEMENT = ['low', 'medium', 'high']\n\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_from_stimulus_onset', 'trial_number_in_block']\nOUTPUT_NAMES = ['choice', 'prior_probability_left', 'wheel_speed', 'whisker_motion_energy']\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [['left', 'right'], ['0.2', '0.5', '0.8'], MOVEMENT, MOVEMENT]\n\n# the cache location is not known until --datadir is parsed, and the connection cannot be\n# shared across a fork anyway, so connect() fills this in per process rather than at import\none = None\nsubset_csv = None    # DATALIMIT_SUBSET.csv path, or None on the full dataset; set by connect()\nbrain_regions = BrainRegions()\n\n\ndef connect(datadir):\n    \"\"\"Point the module-level ONE client at the cache under datadir.\n\n    An Alyx-backed client is required: eid2pid, which load_neural() uses to find the probe\n    insertions, exists only on OneAlyx. mode='local' returns a plain One without it. The\n    client also resolves each dataset's current revision, which is what is on disk -- the\n    release tables list the pre-revision paths, so resolving from them alone finds no\n    trials. The metadata that resolution needs is cached under one_cache/.rest, so a run\n    does not have to reach Alyx.\n\n    datadir: directory holding the one_cache/ folder.\n    Sets the globals `one` and `subset_csv`; returns nothing.\n    \"\"\"\n    global one\n    global subset_csv\n    cache = os.path.join(datadir, ONE_CACHE_DIRNAME)\n    tables = os.path.join(cache, RELEASE)\n    client = dict(base_url=BASE_URL, silent=True, cache_dir=cache, tables_dir=tables,\n                  mode='remote')\n    try:\n        # No password: passing one forces re-authentication over the network, while the\n        # token the fetch cached needs no connection.\n        one = ONE(**client)\n    except Exception:\n        one = ONE(password=PASSWORD, **client)\n    one.alyx.default_expiry = REST_EXPIRY\n    # One.load_cache reads the parquet tables where they are; the OneAlyx override would\n    # ask Alyx for a newer copy first. The ONE\n    # release index is unmodified and still lists every released session, so\n    # restrict to the eids named there -- otherwise a session that is not on disk\n    # would be fetched over the network. The full dataset has no such file, and every\n    # session the index lists is on disk.\n    # Compare in string space: one.search returns UUID objects while the csv column\n    # is str, so a plain set intersection is empty whatever the contents. keep must\n    # stay UUID-valued for the `eid in keep` test below.\n    if subset_csv is not None:\n        subset_eids = set(pd.read_csv(subset_csv).eid.astype(str))\n        keep = {eid for eid in keep if str(eid) in subset_eids}\n        if not keep:\n            raise SystemExit(f'No sessions matched {subset_csv}; refusing to continue.')\n\n    eids, info = one.search(query_type='local', details=True)\n    selected = {}\n    for eid, session in zip(eids, info):\n        if eid in keep:\n            selected.setdefault(session['subject'], []).append(str(eid))\n    return {subject: selected[subject] for subject in sorted(selected)}\n\n\ndef camera_view(eid):\n    \"\"\"The side camera this session has whisker motion energy for, left preferred.\"\"\"\n    for view in ('left', 'right'):\n        if len(one.list_datasets(eid, filename=f'{view}Camera.ROIMotionEnergy.npy',\n                                 query_type='local')):\n            return view\n    raise ValueError(f'no whisker motion energy for {eid}')\n\n\n# --- trials ---\n\ndef trial_variables(trials):\n    \"\"\"Choice, block prior and trial number in block, one row per trial.\"\"\"\n    # NaN compares false, so those go too\n    keep &= trials.choice.isin(CHOICE).to_numpy()               # drops the no response trials\n    keep &= trials.probabilityLeft.isin(PRIOR).to_numpy()\n\n    return keep & covered(wheel_times, stim_on) & covered(camera_times, stim_on)\n\n\n# --- behavior ---\n\ndef window_slice(times, stim_on):\n    \"\"\"Index range of each trial window, so a stream is sliced rather than rescanned per trial.\"\"\"\n    window_start = stim_on + T_START\n    window_stop = stim_on + T_STOP\n\n    # the samples are in time order, so each window is one contiguous range of them\n    begin = np.searchsorted(times, window_start)\n    end = np.searchsorted(times, window_stop)\n\n    return begin, end\n\n\ndef trial_traces(times, values, stim_on):\n    \"\"\"A continuous trace resampled onto the same time grid for every trial.\"\"\"\n    begin, end = window_slice(times, stim_on)\n\n    traces = []\n    for trial, onset in enumerate(stim_on):\n        # skip the md5 check, which rereads every spike file and draws its own progress bar\n        spikes, clusters, channels = loader.load_spike_sorting(check_hash=False)\n\n        # a session can hold an insertion whose spike sorting was never released\n        if not clusters:\n            continue\n\n        clusters = loader.merge_clusters(spikes, clusters, channels)   # Beryl is the coarser atlas the reference code uses, e.g. DG-sg and DG-mo both become DG\n        regions.extend(brain_regions.acronym2acronym(clusters['acronym'][is_good], mapping='Beryl'))\n\n    times, units = np.concatenate(times), np.concatenate(units)\n\n    # sort the merged probes by spike time, as the reference does, so trials can be sliced\n    order = np.argsort(times, kind='stable')\n    return times[order], units[order], np.array(regions)\n\n\ndef spike_counts(times, units, n_units, stim_on):\n    \"\"\"Spike count per unit and bin, for every trial.\"\"\"\n    counts = np.empty((stim_on.size, n_units, N_BINS))\n    begin, end = window_slice(times, stim_on)\n\n    for trial, onset in enumerate(stim_on):\n        spike_time = times[begin[trial]:end[trial]] - onset      # time from stimulus onset\n        spike_unit = units[begin[trial]:end[trial]]\n\n        bin_index = np.floor((spike_time - T_START) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n        \n        # a spike sitting on the window edge can round out of range once the onset is subtracted\n        bin_index = np.clip(bin_index, 0, N_BINS - 1)\n\n        # no trial survived the mask, so there is nothing to load or bin\n    if stim_on.size == 0:\n        return {'session_id': str(eid), 'subject': subject, 'camera': view,\n                'neural': [], 'input': [], 'output': [],\n                'n_trials': 0, 'n_units': 0, 'regions': np.array([])}\n\n    speed = trial_traces(wheel.times, np.abs(wheel.velocity), stim_on)\n    whisker = trial_traces(motion_energy.times, motion_energy.iloc[:, 1], stim_on)\n\n    spike_times, spike_units, regions = load_neural(eid)\n    rate = spike_counts(spike_times, spike_units, regions.size, stim_on) / BIN\n\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Convert the IBL Brain-Wide Map release to the decoder interchange format.\n\nProcessing choices follow code_zhang2025/src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py: BWM release\nsessions/probes, all sorted clusters (qc=None), valid trials with finite essential\ntimestamps, no choice==0 trials, maximum goCue-to-feedback duration 10 s, and\n100 20-ms bins spanning [-0.5, 1.5) s relative to stimulus onset.
